# Hospital Bills in India: Cost Drivers, Markup Economics, and Tariff Regulations


As private clinical markups drive catastrophic out-of-pocket spending, federal friction stalls judicial efforts to standardize inpatient hospital charges.


Health Sector


Statutory, Regulatory And Quasi Judicial Bodies


Government Policies And Interventions For Development In Various Sectors


Oct, 2026


•


13 min read


Inpatient billing in private tertiary hospitals remains driven by unbundled consumables and tiered service tariffs.


### Overview


Private hospital bills in India remain **prohibitively expensive** . Commercial clinical establishments leverage unregulated consumables, bundled procedural tariffs, and tiered room rents to generate wide operating margins. Statutory price controls cover only a narrow basket of essential medicines.


According to National Health Accounts estimates, out-of-pocket expenditure accounted for **39.4% of Total Health Expenditure** in FY 2021-22. Inpatient medical purchases drive the bulk of this household financial distress.


The Supreme Court has pushed to standardise treatment tariffs under the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010. However, public health remains an **Entry 6 State List subject** . This division creates a fragmented regulatory landscape across Indian states.


## Why in the News? The Crisis of Out-of-Pocket Medical Costs


The Supreme Court of India intervened in February 2024 to address escalating inpatient charges across private clinical establishments. A bench hearing *Veterans Forum for Transparency in Public Interest v. Union of India* issued a stern warning to the executive. It cautioned that it would enforce Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) package rates nationwide if the Union government failed to notify standardised treatment charges under **Rule 9(ii)** of the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.


The escalating dispute involves key institutional developments across all three branches of state:


- **Judicial Warning (February 2024):** The Supreme Court threatened nationwide CGHS rate imposition under **Rule 9(ii)** if the executive failed to act.
- **Executive Counter-Affidavit (August 2024):** The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare defended Rule 9(ii) as a state duty under **Article 47 of the Constitution** , arguing clinical care cannot operate as an unfettered commercial enterprise.
- **Parliamentary Scrutiny (August 2026):** The 176th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare revealed that average private hospitalisation costs (₹50,508) are nearly **eight times higher** than public facility costs (₹6,631).


As of August 2024, the policy friction between judicial enforcement and private hospital viability remains unresolved.


National Health Accounts data shows Out-of-Pocket Expenditure (OOPE) dropped from **64.2% in 2013-14 to 39.4% in 2021-22** . Even with that drop, unexpected medical emergencies remain a primary catalyst for household debt.

## Inside the Patient Bill: What Drives the Final Cost?


Inpatient bills in private tertiary hospitals stem mainly from pharmaceutical products, diagnostic investigations, and variable infrastructure fees. Direct doctor compensation accounts for only a minor share of the invoice. An investigation by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) revealed that non-scheduled medicines, surgical devices, and consumables comprise an **average of 46%** of total hospital billing.


Private healthcare institutions operate as bundled service providers. When an individual undergoes surgical intervention, the final statement amalgamates procedural charges, pharmacy costs, biomedical waste handling fees, and nursing services.


Billing Component Proportion of Inpatient Bill Primary Cost Driver Regulatory Status


**Non-Scheduled Consumables & Devices** ~46% Syringes, gloves, IV sets, catheters, surgical packs Uncapped retail margins; subject to 10% annual price-hike ceiling


**Scheduled Essential Formulations** ~10%–15% Basic antibiotics, analgesics, emergency cardiac drugs Ceiling price fixed by NPPA under DPCO, 2013


**Room Accommodation & Nursing** ~20%–25% Bed category tiers (General, Deluxe, Suite) Entirely unregulated; acts as multiplier for clinical fees


**Diagnostic & Laboratory Investigations** ~10%–15% Imaging (MRI/CT), pathology tests Unregulated at national level; facility-determined tariffs


**Consultation & Surgical Fees** ~10%–15% Operating surgeon, anaesthetist, daily rounds Facility-dependent; professional fee schedules


This structural breakdown demonstrates that institutional profits rely on **consumable items and bed fees** . Direct clinical care constitutes a minor fraction of the billing profile.


Anatomy of an inpatient bill: consumables, diagnostic tests, and accommodation charges comprise the bulk of total expenses.


## The Markup Machine: How Medicines and Consumables Inflate Inpatient Bills


Medical consumables and non-scheduled pharmaceuticals are primary profit centres for commercial hospital operators due to extreme retail supply chain margins. The NPPA revealed profit margins on non-scheduled consumables reaching **up to 1,737%** during an investigation into private billing. The agency documented a fatal dengue treatment case at Fortis Hospital Gurugram, where the patient's family was billed for **616 syringes and 1,500 non-sterile gloves** over 15 days.


Hospitals secure substantial institutional discounts through bulk procurement from manufacturers. However, facilities print high Maximum Retail Prices (MRPs) on packaged consumables and bill inpatients at the full retail price. A market survey highlighted by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported hospital markup ratios **exceeding 2,800%** . It cited intravenous infusion sets procured for ₹11.05 and billed to patients at an MRP of ₹325.


The Competition Commission of India (CCI) evaluated these commercial practices in May 2026. The commission closed a decade-long antitrust inquiry against 12 Delhi super-speciality hospitals in *Vivek Sharma v. Becton Dickinson & Ors.* . The CCI ruled that captive in-house pharmacies do not constitute a separate relevant market because hospitals deliver bundled clinical care. The Commission observed that high consumer costs stem from a **regulatory vacuum** , as no statutory statute mandates private providers to pass bulk procurement discounts to patients.


Where regulatory interventions have occurred, trade margin rationalisation has delivered measurable consumer relief:


- **Cardiac Stents Price Caps (2017):** The NPPA invoked public-interest emergency powers under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013. The regulator capped bare-metal stents at ₹7,260 and drug-eluting stents at ₹29,600, slashing prices by **up to 85%** after exposing supply chain markups exceeding 400%.
- **Anti-Cancer Medicine Pilot (2019):** Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) capped margins at 30% for 42 non-scheduled oncology drugs, reducing MRPs by **up to 91%** across 526 brands and yielding annual consumer savings of approximately ₹984 crore.
- **Expanded Oncology Price Caps (October 2026):** The Union Government decided to cap trade margins at 30% for 110 non-scheduled cancer drugs, but the list was still being finalised as reported on 8 October 2026.

## Room Rents and Service Multipliers: The Hidden Economics of Hospital Stays


Proportional billing models permit healthcare providers to inflate overall procedural costs based solely on the inpatient room category chosen by the patient. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare highlighted this practice in its 176th Report.


Patients admitted to executive suites or deluxe private rooms encounter dynamic pricing markups. Operating theatre fees, doctor consultation rounds, and specialist charges escalate proportionately. Yet the underlying surgical equipment, clinical inputs, and surgeon time remain identical.


Hospital administrators justify these price multipliers as internal cross-subsidies for institutional overheads and concession beds. In practice, this mechanism distorts clinical costing. It inflates out-of-pocket obligations for families carrying private health insurance.


Insurance policies frequently feature **room rent sub-limits** , typically capped at 1% of the total sum insured per day. When a patient selects a room exceeding that limit, insurers apply proportionate deductions across the entire bill. This clause forces families to shoulder unexpected co-payments.


The 176th Parliamentary Report urged structural reform of inpatient lodging fees through two specific mechanisms:


- **Tariff Benchmarking:** Benchmarking metropolitan private hospital room tariffs to the average rates of local **three-star hotel accommodations** .
- **Mandatory Fee Unbundling:** Delinking diagnostic, nursing, and procedural charges from physical lodging fees to curb proportional cost escalation.


Proportional pricing functions as a tariff multiplier, escalating procedural fees based solely on room category.


## Existing Guardrails: How DPCO, NPPA, and the Clinical Establishments Act Function


Statutory oversight over medical billing is divided between national drug pricing regimes and fragmented state-level clinical establishment acts. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority regulates essential medicines through the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, which is promulgated under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.


For formulations listed in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), the NPPA establishes ceiling prices based on the simple average of market brands that maintain at least a **1% value market share** . Conversely, non-scheduled medicines and medical devices remain exempt from direct ceiling prices. Manufacturers and hospitals are permitted to raise their MRPs by up to **10% annually** under Paragraph 20 of the DPCO.


Regulatory Sphere Primary Authority & Statutory Base Core Powers & Enforcement Limitations


**Union Government** NPPA via DPCO, 2013 (Essential Commodities Act, 1955) Fixes ceiling prices on scheduled NLEM formulations; caps non-scheduled drug price hikes at 10% annually; no mandate to cap overall hospital procedure charges.


**State Legislatures** State Health Departments via Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 Empowered under Rule 9(ii) to enforce standard service rates; unenforceable in states that have not adopted the central statute (such as Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu).


The primary legislative instrument for clinical tariffs is the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010. Under Rule 9(ii) of the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012, registered facilities must levy charges within a rate band determined by the Central Government in consultation with State Governments.


However, Public Health is an **Entry 6 subject** under List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. Parliament enacted the Clinical Establishments Act under Article 252, which requires state legislatures to pass enabling resolutions before the statute takes effect. Major states with extensive private healthcare sectors—including Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu—have not adopted the federal statute. These states maintain local legislation that rarely mandates standardised procedure rates.


Several regional regulatory frameworks have attempted alternative tariff models:


1. **West Bengal Regulatory Commission Model:** Operating under the West Bengal Clinical Establishments Act, 2017, the West Bengal Clinical Establishment Regulatory Commission (WBCERC) issued Advisory No. 20/2020. This advisory capped doctor consultation charges and mandated **minimum discounts of 10%** on medicines and 20% on consumables relative to printed MRPs.
2. **Rajasthan Right to Health Framework:** The Rajasthan Right to Health Act, 2023 established an enforceable statutory right to emergency medical treatment without out-of-pocket prepayment, requiring the state government to reimburse clinical facilities at **fixed package tariffs** .

## Why Price Controls Fall Short in Regulating Private Hospitals


Uniform price ceilings frequently fail in private hospital settings because clinical providers bypass price caps through substitution and cost shifting. When the NPPA imposed statutory price caps on coronary stents in 2017, several hospitals increased charges for catheterisation laboratories, nursing care, and post-operative monitoring to protect aggregate procedural margins.


The Indian Medical Association (IMA) opposed rigid national procedural price ceilings before the Supreme Court in *Veterans Forum for Transparency in Public Interest* . The association argued that clinical operating costs vary substantially across geographical locations.


Operating expenses in Tier-1 metropolitan centres differ from Tier-2 and rural districts due to four distinct cost drivers:


- **Real Estate Overheads:** Higher land acquisition costs and steep commercial rentals in urban metros;
- **Capital Expenditures:** Heavy upfront investments in advanced diagnostic and therapeutic hardware;
- **Accreditation Mandates:** Rigorous compliance requirements for National Accreditation Board for Hospitals (NABH) standards;
- **Specialist Compensation:** Market-driven salaries necessary to recruit and retain super-specialist doctors.


A blunt national price ceiling risks discouraging capital reinvestment, lowering clinical standards, and encouraging the informal rejection of complex, high-risk surgical cases. Clinical care cannot be commoditised into rigid price bands without accounting for patient comorbidities and secondary complications.


Regional variations in land, equipment capital expenditure, and human resources complicate uniform national price caps.


## Ethics and Governance: Information Asymmetry and the Right to Health


Market failures in private healthcare stem from severe information asymmetry between medical practitioners and vulnerable patients. In his 1963 economic treatise, Kenneth Arrow established that medical transactions deviate fundamentally from **conventional competitive markets** . Patients lack the specialised knowledge required to evaluate clinical recommendations during acute illness.


This dynamic generates **supplier-induced demand** , where the healthcare provider simultaneously dictates the demand for diagnostic services and supplies the paid treatment. Bereft of price transparency, distressed families cannot negotiate medical charges or question consumption volumes for consumables such as syringes, infusion sets, and laboratory profiles.


Market Actor Structural Position Operational Consequence


**Patient in Distress** Lacks diagnostic expertise; exhibits inelastic demand for survival Incapable of price negotiation; absorbs arbitrary procedural costs


**Healthcare Provider** Possesses clinical monopoly; acts as both advisor and merchant Directs supplier-induced demand; bills for captive pharmacy consumables


This commercial structure creates friction with Indian constitutional jurisprudence. The Supreme Court has repeatedly expanded the fundamental Right to Life under Article 21 to encompass healthcare access:


- In *Paschim Banga Khet Majoor Samity v. State of West Bengal* (1996), the Supreme Court ruled that providing timely medical treatment to preserve human life is an **absolute obligation** of the welfare state under Article 21.
- In *Consumer Education & Research Centre v. Union of India* (1995), the Court held that health and medical care represent **fundamental rights under Article 21** read alongside Directive Principles Articles 39(e), 41, 43, and 48A.


Directive Principles under Part IV remain non-justiciable governance goals, but judicial interpretation has tied them to **enforceable fundamental rights** under Part III. Excessive hospital billing that deprives citizens of life-saving care directly undermines this constitutional framework.


## Way Forward: Transparent Costing, Standard Packages, and Stronger Oversight


Addressing high hospital billing requires scientific costing methodologies, unbundled disclosures, and durable public health infrastructure rather than blunt price freezes.


The Union and State governments can implement structural reforms across five distinct policy levers:


1. **Adopting Empirical Cost Databases:** Policymakers should utilise the National Health System Cost Database developed through the 'Cost of Health Services in India' (CHSI) multi-site study. Executed by the Department of Health Research (ICMR) and PGIMER Chandigarh, this platform established normative costs across 74 secondary and tertiary hospitals in 11 states, providing **empirical reference rates** for procedures.
2. **Transitioning to Bundled Case Rates:** Regulators should adapt the Health Benefit Package (HBP) tariff model deployed under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. Managed by the National Health Authority, this framework bundles pre-operative, consumable, implant, and post-operative charges into **single case tariffs** across more than 1,900 procedures, limiting unbundled add-on billing.
3. **Mandatory Upfront Cost Disclosures:** As recommended by the 176th Parliamentary Standing Committee Report, clinical establishments should issue **binding upfront cost estimates** prior to non-emergency inpatient admissions. Private hospitals must also unbundle nursing, accommodation, and procedural fees on final bills.
4. **Targeted Margin Rationalisation:** The Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers should broaden Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) across all non-scheduled consumables and implantable devices, capping markups at the first point of sale to prevent artificial MRP inflation.
5. **Expanding Public Hospital Capacity:** The National Health Policy 2017 targeted an increase in public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025. However, actual Government Health Expenditure stood at **1.43% of GDP** as of FY 2022-23. Enhancing investments in secondary and tertiary public healthcare is essential to provide high-quality alternatives and introduce natural market discipline into private pricing.

## Key Takeaways


- Private inpatient hospital bills in India remain elevated primarily due to unregulated medical consumables, tiered room rent multipliers, and unbundled service charges.
- The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority regulates ceiling prices for essential formulations under the DPCO, 2013, but non-scheduled consumables remain subject only to an annual retail price-hike ceiling of 10%.
- An NPPA billing study exposed hospital profit margins on consumables reaching up to 1,737%, with non-scheduled medicines and consumables comprising an average of 46% of total inpatient bills.
- Standardising private medical procedure charges under Rule 9(ii) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 faces federal barriers because Public Health is an Entry 6 State List subject under the Seventh Schedule.
- The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognised healthcare and emergency preservation of life as integral to the fundamental Right to Life under Article 21 of the Constitution.
- Sustainable solutions require shifting toward standardised bundled packages, applying trade margin caps on hospital consumables, and increasing public health expenditure from 1.43% toward the National Health Policy target of 2.5% of GDP.
